newsitem.title: UK: London gold fixes shade firmer but tone bearish.
newsitem.headline: London gold fixes shade firmer but tone bearish.

text.p: Precious metals were mostly slightly firmer on Friday compared with the previous close as a weaker dollar encouraged buying, especially of gold, dealers said.
Even so the markets were cautious and the mood defensive as dealers and analysts continued to mull the implIcations of Germany revaluing its near 3,000-tonne gold reserve.
Bullion was fixed at $347.00 per ounce, up just 60 cents from Thursday afternoon, reflecting fairly stable prices in New York and the Far East.
But the focus remained on Germany and the proposal to revalue its reserves from around $95 per ounce to nearer market price.
The plan was part of strategy to help plug a multi-billion mark hole in the country's 1997 budget.
"Some very responsible central banks are talking about their gold reserves," one dealer said. "They know the implications for the market so they have to be serious to say something."

Earlier this year, Switzerland, the only country with a significant percentage of its note issue backed by gold, announced plans to revalue reserves of 2,500 tonnes and reduce the amount of gold backing required by the Swiss franc.
Part of the gold released would be sold and the cash surplus used to establish a humanitarian fund.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel stated on Thursday that no gold would be sold from the Bundesbank's reserves but this was not reassuring for the market.
"If a country has its gold assets valued closer to the market price, then it will have to manage the assets to a far greater degree than it does at present," a dealer said.
"If it can see there is no return on that asset, the logical step is to sell it and replace it with something which does bring a return," the dealer said.
Technically gold's outlook was weakening too after establishing a $346-$351 price range earlier in the week.
"We had a bull flag formation earlier but it has turned a bit pear-shaped now having hit a lower high all week and a new low each day," a dealer said.
But he added that when the price had dipped to around $346.00, good buying support had come into the market.
Silver was quiet and down two cents at $4.84/$4.85 while platinum was up $0.75 at $393.75/$394.75 and palladium was $0.50 higher at $173.00/$174.00.
Dealers said the the platinum group metals were still very tight for lack of Russian exports, and prices were volatile.
